claim: Sleep is a ubiquitous state in animals.
source: Sleep is a ubiquitous state in animals (Anafi et al., 2019) that is controlled by an ensemble of nuclei and their brain-wide interactions (Pace-Schott and Hobson, 2002; Sakai, 2020; Saper et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anafi et al., 2019

claim: Sleep is controlled by an ensemble of nuclei and their brain-wide interactions.
source: Sleep is a ubiquitous state in animals (Anafi et al., 2019) that is controlled by an ensemble of nuclei and their brain-wide interactions (Pace-Schott and Hobson, 2002; Sakai, 2020; Saper et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pace-Schott and Hobson, 2002; Sakai, 2020; Saper et al., 2010

claim: In mammals, sleep is broadly comprised of two stages: non-rapid eye movement (NREM or slow-wave sleep) and rapid eye movement (REM or paradoxical sleep).
source: In mammals (Cirelli, 2009), sleep is broadly comprised of two stages: non-rapid eye movement (NREM or slow-wave sleep) and rapid eye movement (REM or paradoxical sleep) (Weber and Dan, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cirelli, 2009 and Weber and Dan, 2016

claim: During NREM sleep, there are broad-band increases in the local field potential (LFP) power in the cortex that are modulated at <1 Hz.
source: During NREM sleep, there are broad-band increases in the local field potential (LFP) power in the cortex that are modulated at <1 Hz (Amzica and Steriade, 1998; Datta and Maclean, 2007; Saper and Fuller, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Amzica and Steriade, 1998; Datta and Maclean, 2007; Saper and Fuller, 2017

claim: During REM sleep, gamma band power (nominally 30–100 Hz) is elevated in the cortex.
source: During REM sleep, gamma band power (nominally 30–100 Hz) is elevated in the cortex (Cantero et al., 2004; Le Van Quyen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cantero et al., 2004; Le Van Quyen et al., 2010

claim: In the hippocampus, REM sleep is associated with a marked increase in power in the theta band (nominally 4–10 Hz) in rodents.
source: In the hippocampus, REM sleep is also associated with a marked increase in power in the theta band (nominally 4–10 Hz) in rodents (Montgomery et al., 2008; Sullivan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Montgomery et al., 2008; Sullivan et al., 2014

claim: Pioneering studies using positron-emission tomography (PET) or 133Xenon in humans have suggested that cerebral blood flow (CBF) and metabolism is reduced during NREM sleep as compared with those during awake levels.
source: Pioneering studies using positron-emission tomography (PET) or 133Xenon in humans have suggested that cerebral blood flow (CBF) and metabolism is reduced during NREM sleep as compared with those during awake levels, and increased above said levels during REM sleep (Braun et al., 1997; Townsend et al., 1973), though the temporal and spatial resolutions of these techniques are poor.
evidence: Supported by citations to Braun et al., 1997; Townsend et al., 1973

claim: Pioneering studies using positron-emission tomography (PET) or 133Xenon in humans have suggested that cerebral blood flow (CBF) and metabolism is increased above awake levels during REM sleep.
source: Pioneering studies using positron-emission tomography (PET) or 133Xenon in humans have suggested that cerebral blood flow (CBF) and metabolism is reduced during NREM sleep as compared with those during awake levels, and increased above said levels during REM sleep (Braun et al., 1997; Townsend et al., 1973), though the temporal and spatial resolutions of these techniques are poor.
evidence: Supported by citations to Braun et al., 1997; Townsend et al., 1973

claim: The temporal and spatial resolutions of PET and 133Xenon techniques are poor.
source: Pioneering studies using positron-emission tomography (PET) or 133Xenon in humans have suggested that cerebral blood flow (CBF) and metabolism is reduced during NREM sleep as compared with those during awake levels, and increased above said levels during REM sleep (Braun et al., 1997; Townsend et al., 1973), though the temporal and spatial resolutions of these techniques are poor.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of the cited techniques

claim: The degree to which CBF changes during the different sleep states appears dependent upon brain region.
source: The degree to which CBF changes during the different sleep states appears dependent upon brain region (Madsen et al., 1991; Maquet and Phillips, 1998), complicating the interpretation of functional connectivity studies looking at correlations between brain regions where subjects may be transitioning among arousal states (Gu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Madsen et al., 1991; Maquet and Phillips, 1998

claim: Several fMRI studies have shown significant alterations in hemodynamic signals and functional connectivity during NREM sleep.
source: Several fMRI studies have shown significant alterations in hemodynamic signals and functional connectivity during NREM sleep (Boly et al., 2012; Dang-Vu et al., 2008; Fukunaga et al., 2006; Horovitz et al., 2008; Larson-Prior et al., 2009; Mitra et al., 2015), suggesting that the blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signal changes during sleep.
evidence: Supported by citations to Boly et al., 2012; Dang-Vu et al., 2008; Fukunaga et al., 2006; Horovitz et al., 2008; Larson-Prior et al., 2009; Mitra et al., 2015

claim: The blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signal changes during sleep.

evidence: Inferred from fMRI studies showing alterations in hemodynamic signals during NREM sleep

claim: BOLD signals are generated by a complicated interplay of cerebral metabolism and changes in blood flow and volume.
source: Because BOLD signals are generated by a complicated interplay of cerebral metabolism and changes in blood flow and volume (Kim and Ogawa, 2012), the vascular basis of these changes and their relation to neural activity are not well understood.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Ogawa, 2012

claim: Functional ultrasound measures indicate cerebral blood volume rises during sleep.
source: Although functional ultrasound measures indicate cerebral blood volume rises during sleep (likely due to arterial dilation Mateo et al., 2017) and is correlated with hippocampal theta and gamma band power (Bergel et al., 2018), the relationship of cortical vascular changes to local cortical neural activity is unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mateo et al., 2017

claim: The rise in cerebral blood volume during sleep is likely due to arterial dilation.

claim: BOLD signal changes during sleep are associated with movement of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

evidence: Supported by citation to Fultz et al., 2019
